papers.title: VASTRA: Efficient Agentic Top-K Interactive Video Analysis
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable natural language video retrieval, bypassing traditional hand-engineered pipelines. Integrating agentic reasoning frameworks (e.g., ReAct) further advances this paradigm by allowing models to dynamically inspect video content rather than relying on a single visual pass. Applying this pattern naively to video retrieval inherits problems that video systems cannot afford: results vary from run to run under identical conditions, and cost and latency scale with every reasoning step the agent takes rather than with the work the query actually requires. We present VASTRA, an agentic video retrieval system whose execution is dictated by query complexity rather than an open-ended reasoning loop: cheap, reliably answerable queries are ranked directly from pre-ingested summaries, while harder queries trigger targeted verification only where relevance is genuinely uncertain. This keeps control flow external to the model rather than latent in a growing chain of thought, establishing deterministic control flow by construction and end-to-end rank reproducibility under greedy serving. Across 40 benchmark queries, VASTRA exposes explicit presets: VASTRA-Fast runs 12.2x faster (4.2 s vs. 51.2 s) and 10.4x cheaper ($0.0044 vs. $0.0458) than best performing ReAct agent at a 5.0-point mAP reduction, while VASTRA-Max matches peak ReAct agent accuracy (0.653 vs. 0.649 mAP) at comparable latency, trading higher spend ($0.1022 vs. $0.0458) for zero run-to-run variance.

papers.title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone. This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection. We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features. The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

papers.title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
papers.abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.

papers.title: Auriga: Harness-Governed LLM Agents for Effective Throughput Optimization in Execute-Order-Validate Permissioned Blockchains
papers.abstract: Effective throughput, the product of raw throughput and transaction success rate, determines the useful capacity of Execute-Order-Validate blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric. Most prior work either tunes configurations to raise raw throughput, requiring many costly redeployments, or controls conflicts to raise the success rate, repairing them only after execution with kernel modifications. The few joint approaches tune only a small set of parameters and still rely on kernel changes to resolve conflicts. To address these challenges, we present Auriga, a non-invasive framework that jointly optimizes both factors through sample-efficient LLM-guided configuration search and pre-execution conflict prevention. A harness-governed multi-agent architecture coordinates LLM agents for parameter exploration, saturation-aware evaluation, and experience consolidation, with the harness controlling tool and memory access and retaining termination authority. For transaction scheduling, an LLM extracts symbolic AST templates from smart contracts offline. At runtime, the scheduler predicts read-write sets without executing them and partitions transactions into conflict-free groups. Across three benchmarks and conflict rates up to 70%, Auriga improves effective throughput by up to 6.0 times over default Fabric and 2.0 times over the strongest baseline. The tuning agent also discovers undocumented parameter dependencies, and ablation studies show the independent contributions of both subsystems.

papers.title: VecDBLens: An Evaluatology-Based Framework for Vector Database Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Vector databases are increasingly deployed as retrieval pipelines in which representation, indexing, and query-time execution jointly determine accuracy, throughput, and cost. Existing vector database evaluations primarily focus on indexing while treating embeddings as fixed inputs and ignoring the role of query-time execution, making it difficult to decide whether a bottleneck should be addressed by changing the embedding model, the index, or the query-processing functions. To address the above limitation, we introduce VecDBLens, an Evaluatology-based framework that treats the function under diagnosis as an evaluated object and all remaining dataset, workload, parameter, and runtime factors as matched evaluation conditions. VecDBLens attributes performance differences to individual evaluated objects through comparisons under matched evaluation conditions, summarizing their performance and stability across multiple datasets and workloads. It further analyzes interactions among objects using analysis of variance (ANOVA), thereby turning vector database benchmarking from leaderboard ranking into a reproducible diagnostic procedure. VecDBLens reveals two key insights. First, retrieval performance is fundamentally upper-bounded by embedding quality, revealing that many apparent indexing failures are therefore representation-side limitations. Second, stronger index parameterization is not always beneficial: overly aggressive configurations can reshape neighborhood topology and cause recall regression. These results challenge the common practice of evaluating vector databases primarily through indexing and show that real-world limitations arise from constraints across retrieval functions rather than any single function alone. VecDBLens provides a principled basis for identifying the true performance drivers of vector databases and for guiding their design in practical applications.

papers.title: Beyond Symmetry: Asymmetric Matching with Transformers for Collective Entity Resolution
papers.abstract: A core assumption of entity resolution (ER) is its symmetric nature, which rests on a principle so self-evident it borders on tautology: if a refers to the same object as b, then b must also refer to the same object as a. However, this global property of symmetry does not necessarily extend to each of the complex decision processes within ER systems. In cases involving vague or ambiguous information, enforcing symmetry can be detrimental to performance, an issue exemplified by the ``bad triplet problem''. This paper investigates the effects of input-order asymmetry within a collective ER framework that integrates distinct matching and clustering stages. The input order-aware matching stage utilizes pre-trained transformers to explicitly model and exploit asymmetry, making it possible to evaluate its effect on clustering performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that asymmetry is not only measurable but also introduces a significant skew in the final entity clusters, highlighting the need to re-evaluate supervised training methodologies for matchers, particularly the development of direction-aware training paradigms that can preserve, rather than neutralize, the inherent asymmetry in matching tasks.

papers.title: Probe-Based Routing for Join Optimizer Selection
papers.abstract: In optimizers that choose a join-order solver by a size rule, join ordering is an algorithm-selection problem, because dynamic programming (DP), genetic search (GEQO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) each win on different queries. PostgreSQL nevertheless chooses among them by relation count alone, although queries with the same relation count can favor different solvers. This paper introduces two landscape features that a probe computes from random join orders in microseconds per query. The tail spacing $\alpha$ describes how the costs of the best sampled orders are spaced, and the crossover surprise $\theta$ describes how far the cost of a crossover child deviates from the mean cost of its parents. The router clusters training queries by these features and the relation count, assigns a solver to every cluster that this solver wins in total end-to-end time by a margin, and leaves all other queries to PostgreSQL's default rule. On JOB and IMDb-CEB, the router lowers mean end-to-end time relative to the default rule, and on IMDb-CEB the probe features nearly double the gain obtained from the relation count alone, so they carry information about the queries that the relation count lacks.

papers.title: Optimal-Time Independent Subset Sampling over Acyclic Joins
papers.abstract: Join results can greatly exceed their inputs even when applications need only a small random subset. We study sampling that includes each result independently with a prescribed probability given by the product of its input-tuple weights (PRODUCT). For fixed full acyclic joins with static weights, we achieve input-linear preprocessing and index space together with output-linear expected sampling work, eliminating logarithmic factors from previous bounds. A shared join-tree index supports weighted draws over the entire join and locates high-probability results. Direct Bernoulli trials handle high-probability results, allowing Poisson thinning to generate the remaining independent inclusion decisions with bounded overhead. Our exact sampler uses expected $O(N)$ preprocessing, $O(N)$ index space, and expected $O(1+m\mu)$ time per call including output construction. Here $N$ is the input size, $m$ counts relation occurrences, and $\mu$ is the expected sample size. The guarantees hold on a real random-access machine with unit-cost exact arithmetic and logarithms, continuous uniform randomness, and expected-time hashing. The time bounds are optimal, matching input reading and explicit output writing. Our floating-point prototype has lower sampling latency than the fastest applicable baseline in 17 of 18 PRODUCT settings on three queries over the STATS benchmark. Construction savings on large joins can offset indexed materialization's faster sampling over a limited number of calls. On a real-data path at $\mu=100$, our sampler achieves a $20.5\times$ speedup over indexed materialization for construction plus 300 calls, measured after common data preparation and loading.

papers.title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data
papers.abstract: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. We present HeriKGQA, a knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, leaving computation to SPARQL and deterministic code. Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology aligning W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results and temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer, with error correction guarding each LLM step. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.

papers.title: Towards Unified File Management for Data Lakehouse Systems
papers.abstract: Data lakehouse systems have garnered widespread adoption, yet their metadata management systems face a fundamental architectural dilemma. File-based OTFs (Open Table Formats) scale well, but suffer from metadata bloat, high commit latencies, the absence of multi-table transactions, and unsafe garbage collection. On the other hand, catalogs relying entirely on a transactional database incur severe scalability bottlenecks due to analytic file-level metadata. To reconcile this tension, we present Raven, an operational catalog that stores transactional metadata within a database while offloading analytical metadata to underlying OTF structures. Based on this hybrid architecture, Raven introduces an extended Merge-on-Read (MoR) mechanism to reduce commit latency and mitigate metadata bloat, alongside multi-table transactions under snapshot isolation. Furthermore, Raven unifies core data lakehouse semantics including versioning and reference tracking under an extensible ER (Entity-Relationship) metadata model, enabling safe global garbage collection across diverse types of assets. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Raven substantially reduces commit latency and metadata bloat when integrated with Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, maintains a catalog storage footprint orders of magnitude smaller than database-only systems like DuckLake, and achieves scalable garbage collection with minimal disruption.

papers.title: REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
papers.abstract: Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled. Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

papers.title: Calibrated Early Termination with Bounded Optimality Gaps for Constrained Vector Search
papers.abstract: Vector search over learned embeddings is the retrieval layer of recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation, and many applications cap how many answer items one category may contribute. Graph indexes answer a query by best-first traversal, and where it stops determines its cost and whether its answer is exact. We study early termination for such constrained $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) queries, with plain $k$-NN as a special case, and seek the cheapest stopping rule whose answer is exact with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Learned early-termination methods instead target average recall, which does not guarantee exact answers. Multiple testing can calibrate any parameterized stopping rule to our target, but it cannot tell how much a better rule with the same risk and observations would save. Answering this needs a lower bound on the optimum of a rule family too large to enumerate, valid for the query population. Our key idea is to declare the observations a rule may use and to consider every rule monotone in them. Risk-constrained stopping then becomes a linear program over an order polytope, whose Lagrangian minimizers form a nested chain of staircase rules computed exactly by dynamic programming. Fixed-sequence binomial tests along this chain calibrate our rule, CaST, whose failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-\delta$. Lagrangian weak duality bounds the optimum of the declared class from below at all risk levels at once, without a union bound over the rules. On two datasets of one million items each, CaST replayed on logged searches costs at most 1.132 times the class optimum for risk levels from 0.03 to 0.10, at 95% joint confidence per setting. Larger savings thus need a rule outside the class. At a common risk target on held-out queries, CaST is faster than every other calibrated rule we time, which take 4.8% to 45.5% more mean time.

papers.title: HyperPage: Learned Page Layouts for Disk-Resident Graph Vector Indexes
papers.abstract: Disk-resident graph indexes such as DiskANN store each vector with its graph edges as one record on SSD pages. A search needs the page of every record it expands, so its page reads depend on the page layout, that is, which records share a page. Search agents trained with reinforcement learning query one such index run after run, and every graph traversal can be logged with the records it expands. We therefore use the logs of a finished run to lay out the index for a declared memory budget, so later runs read fewer pages. In contrast, existing layouts such as Starling and MARGO are computed from the graph and vectors and use no logs. Learning a layout from logs is challenging, because the logs must stay valid under every layout, the saving depends on what the budget caches, and the best layout is NP-hard to find. Our key observation is that DiskANN-style search routes on in-memory codes and the records it expands, never on their page-mates. As a result, the logged traversals price every layout by replay, and cached records add no page reads. Accordingly, we propose HyperPage, which first builds layouts for the declared budget on the logged traversals of uncached records. It then selects one layout, together with the budget split between hot records and a page cache, by replaying validation steps. In addition, a Lagrangian lower bound shows how far a layout may be from the optimum. We learn from one Search-R1 agent run and test on a later run with a different reward, over 1M and 21M passages. Across seven cache budgets, HyperPage reads 5.2% to 21.2% fewer pages than MARGO, and no compared layout reads fewer. The advantage is largest when the cache is small. For example, at 1% of the 1M index, MARGO needs nearly 3 times the budget to read as few pages. On the 21M index, HyperPage also cuts search time per step by up to 10.4%. The saving holds for a second agent model and a second corpus.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Range Counting over Local Graph Statistics
papers.abstract: Range counting over vertex statistics supports contact analysis, community profiling, and reputation screening. However, releasing exact range counts can disclose sensitive edges to an adversary with background knowledge. We study this problem under edge local differential privacy (edge LDP), where each vertex randomizes its report before sending it to an untrusted curator. We develop a layered framework that connects statistic estimation, direct range estimation, and adaptive estimator selection. Statistic-estimation methods provide complementary scalar estimators with explicit loss analyses, while indicator-estimation methods privatize range indicators directly. We next propose Bounded Conditional Range Inversion (BCRI), which derives unbiased range estimates from reusable bounded geometric reports through an explicit local inverse. Its boundary-conditioned estimator achieves no larger expected L2 loss than the unbounded inverse, and histogram preprocessing supports constant-time queries. The same reports also provide a nonnegative, unbiased variance estimate for every answer. At the center of the framework, Adaptive Estimator Selection (AES) privately predicts bias, variance, and covariance to combine BCRI with a conditional estimator from the same transcript. Experiments on diverse real-world graph tasks demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, and workload scalability of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases
papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has become a fundamental query primitive in modern vector databases for managing large-scale embedding data. To support growing vector collections, organizations increasingly outsource database management and query processing to third-party clouds. However, untrusted service providers may return suboptimal or fabricated results, posing a serious threat to ANN search integrity. Existing authenticated ANN approaches face substantial scalability challenges. They typically require transmitting high-dimensional vectors for distance verification and rely on topology-agnostic authentication structures, resulting in excessive communication and verification overhead. In this paper, we propose VIDA, a novel and efficient scheme for authenticated graph-based ANN search. VIDA replaces raw vector transmission with compact vector commitments and employs an aggregated Inner Product Argument to efficiently verify multiple distance computations. Furthermore, we introduce MeST, a topology-aware authenticated data structure that aligns authentication paths with graph traversal, significantly reducing structural proof overhead. Additionally, we design a quantization-aware authentication strategy that exploits distance bounds for pruning, reducing the number of exact distances requiring cryptographic authentication. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed schemes substantially improve the efficiency of authenticated ANN search, achieving up to a $6.6\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency and reducing data transfer time by up to 99.2% compared with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization. Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge

papers.title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
papers.abstract: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

papers.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
papers.abstract: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

papers.title: Stage-Resolved EBV-Induced B-Cell Programs Across CNS Selection and Multiple Sclerosis Compartments
papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is implicated in multiple sclerosis (MS), but whether EBV-conditioned B cells retain stable transcriptional programs after CNS selection remains uncertain. We reanalyzed datasets spanning experimental EBV infection, CNS-homing B cells in humanized mice, early-MS blood, and paired human CSF and blood. A frozen EBV-induced B-cell factor (F12) was transferred without outcome-driven modification and evaluated using anatomical, sequencing-depth, metabolic, coherence-matched, lineage, and exposure controls. F12 did not predict MS activity (AUC=0.487; p=0.489) and was lower in CSF in nine evaluable participants (mean difference -0.0560; coherence-matched p=0.015). It also remained lower in brain than spleen in all five EBV-exposed mice after matched-depth rarefaction (p=0.0313) and coherence-matched calibration (p=0.0225). The splenic TBX21+CXCR3+ transcriptional gate did not reliably represent the state of anatomically selected brain B cells. An enriched 287-gene cross-system bridge lacked B-lineage and EBV-exposure specificity. In human CSF, an early EBV-associated program was depleted (-0.0492; p=0.0197), whereas latency-III and lymphoblastoid cell line-like programs increased (+0.0666; p=0.0092 and +0.0148; p=0.0096, respectively). Opposite early and late program directions persisted after removing shared genes. No external program met the prespecified prospective criterion. These findings support stage- and compartment-dependent remodeling of EBV-associated B-cell transcription rather than persistence of a stable RNA signature. They distinguish cellular trafficking from transcriptional-state preservation and show that cross-system molecular resemblance alone cannot establish ancestry. EBV-directed biomarker studies should integrate host transcription with virologic, clonotypic, antigen-specific, epigenetic, and longitudinal evidence.

papers.title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
papers.abstract: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

papers.title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
papers.abstract: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.

papers.title: Theory-Driven Network Backbones for Bipartite Projections
papers.abstract: Collecting data, including network data, is subject to measurement error. Network backboning is the process of statistically validating each edge in a network to estimate the probability that the edge is born of noisy measurements. The current backboning literature provides approaches in two classes: structural and statistical. The classes differ in many respects, but they share one commonality: the test used to determine whether to filter out noisy edges is data-agnostic; it does not take into account what the network is representing. However, the nodes and edges of all non-synthetic networks correspond to specific real-world entities, whose dynamics determine how the edge-generating process operates. In this paper, we propose the first in a new class of network backboning algorithms: a theory-driven backboning approach that allows us to encode known dynamics into the backboning process. The resulting backbone embeds the encoded theory and produces a network compatible with it, rather than one that obeys a data-agnostic network process, as in the structural and statistical backboning classes. We specifically focus on the case of projecting and backboning a bipartite structure. We do so by allowing users to specify an Agent-Based Model for the two types of agents (nodes) in the network and by performing Simulation-Based Inference to fit the observed bipartite structure and, as a result, reconstruct the true relationships between the two classes of agents. We test our framework both on synthetic data -- where we have perfect information about the edge-generating process -- and in a case study using archaeological data on amphorae retrieved from different archaeological sites. Our approach improves latent-edge recovery over conventional backboning methods in synthetic experiments and reveals interpretable archaeological patterns despite imperfect model fit.

papers.title: Separations Between Submodular-Like Graph Widths
papers.abstract: Many algorithmic frameworks exist for evaluating join queries. They range from simple ones, such as dynamic programming over a single tree decomposition, high-degree-low-degree splitting from graph algorithms, and the degree uniformization of Joglekar and R\'e, to sophisticated ones based on information-theoretic inequalities, such as the PANDA framework for submodular width. Each of these frameworks except high-degree-low-degree splitting comes with a width notion of the query that determines its running-time exponent. We fill this gap by formalizing high-degree-low-degree splitting with $\ell$ degree classes, which gives rise to the degree-splitting width $\mathrm{ds}_\ell$-width. These width notions form a hierarchy, but it was not known whether the more complicated frameworks achieve better worst-case exponents than the simpler ones on any graph query. We study this question for full self-join-free join queries with binary relations, which amounts to colored subgraph isomorphism for a pattern graph $H$. We show that every inequality in the hierarchy $\mathrm{subw} \le \#\mathrm{subw} \le \text{m-width} \le \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}$ can be strict. For instance, $\text{m-width}(K_{3,3}) = 2 < \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}(K_{3,3})$ for every constant $\ell$, so no constant number of degree classes reaches the exponent of degree uniformization. We find the smallest separating patterns, with 8, 9, and 6 nodes, respectively, by an exhaustive search with a software tool that computes these widths via mixed integer linear programming. Along the way, we give a degree-based algorithm that removes the polylogarithmic overhead of degree uniformization when evaluating full join queries. Furthermore, we show that with logarithmically many degree classes, the degree-splitting width coincides with the m-width of Joglekar and R\'e. Finally, we discuss several open problems.

papers.title: CRINN: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms have become increasingly critical for recent AI applications, particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agent-based LLM applications. In this paper, we present CRINN, a new paradigm for ANNS algorithms. CRINN treats ANNS optimization as a reinforcement learning problem where execution speed serves as the reward signal. This approach enables the automatic generation of progressively faster ANNS implementations while maintaining accuracy constraints. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates CRINN's effectiveness across six widely-used NNS benchmark datasets. When compared against state-of-the-art open-source ANNS algorithms, CRINN achieves best performance on three of them (GIST-960-Euclidean, MNIST-784-Euclidean, and GloVe-25-angular), and tied for first place on two of them (SIFT-128-Euclidean and GloVe-25-angular). The implications of CRINN's success reach well beyond ANNS optimization: It validates that LLMs augmented with reinforcement learning can function as an effective tool for automating sophisticated algorithmic optimizations that demand specialized knowledge and labor-intensive manual refinement. Code can be found at https://github.com/ornith-ai/CRINN

papers.title: When AI Classifies: What Counts as Public Administration?
papers.abstract: This study examines how alternative systems of scholarly representation identify and characterize public administration (PA) and artificial intelligence-related PA (AI-in-PA) scholarship. The central question is not which system provides a definitive classification of PA, but how alternative systems of scholarly classification differ in identifying and representing its intellectual boundaries. With an exploratory and comparative analysis of Web of Science and OpenAlex, the study compares five approaches based on author-defined, citation-driven, and AI-assisted representations. The results highlight substantial differences and limited overlap in corpus size, publication type, DOI availability, publishing outlets, temporal patterns, and thematic structure. The alternative approaches tend to produce distinct representations because they identify substantially different bodies of scholarship rather than merely larger or smaller subsets of the same literature. The findings suggest that algorithmic knowledge organization influences how interdisciplinary scholarship is classified, connected, and understood and, epistemologically, how its visibility, structure, and intellectual identity are represented. AI-enabled scholarly classifications are not neutral but interpretative, potentially self-reinforcing, and may constrain the evolution and adaptation of disciplinary boundaries. Human expert judgment therefore remains essential and is complemented rather than replaced by AI-assisted scholarly classification.

papers.title: Evaluating Local Language Model Agents for Data Engineering: An Empirical Software Engineering Study of Mobility Workflows
papers.abstract: Context: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as software and data-engineering assistants, yet evidence about locally deployable open-weight agents remains limited. Existing evaluations often emphasise textual responses or isolated code rather than complete engineering artifacts. Objectives: We evaluate whether local LLM agents can produce correct and reliable data-engineering artifacts, isolate the contribution of a closed-loop workspace and of input-structure knowledge, and examine trade-offs in runtime, cost, and failure behaviour. Methods: We introduce a benchmark of fifteen mobility data-engineering tasks with deterministic checkers for the scripts, tables, structured files, figures, and reports they produce. Sixteen configurations from six model families are evaluated in three conditions (chat-only, chat-schema, agent-with-tools) with five repetitions per model, condition, and task, yielding 3,600 scored attempts on a consumer-grade GPU. Results: A 4-billion-parameter model at 4-bit reaches 77.3%, a 9-billion-parameter model 80.0% within about 6.5 GB, and a 12-billion-parameter model from another family 81.3%, against 98.7% for the highest-scoring configuration, which solves 14 of 15 tasks in all five repetitions. Above two billion parameters the workspace loop raises pass rates by 24.0 to 65.3 points over uninformed one-shot generation, and its contribution exceeds that of the input-structure summary in eleven of fifteen tasks. Conclusion: Open-weight models that fit on one consumer GPU support a meaningful share of data-engineering work once given a workspace loop, although capability still separates usable from unusable configurations and high-stakes outputs need validation. Being mobility-specific and checker-based, the benchmark characterizes the evaluated configurations, not all data-engineering practice.

papers.title: Community Search under Member-Specific Tolerances
papers.abstract: We study community search when each member has its own tolerance for differences in position, as when members of a group interact repeatedly and influence one another. A latitude-consistent community (LCC) contains the query vertex, is connected, has minimum degree at least k, and bounds its diameter by the smallest member tolerance. The bound is exactly the condition under which every interaction in a connected closed group stays accepted under bounded-confidence dynamics for every choice of positive weights. It also prevents rejection under social-judgment dynamics, whereas the pairwise condition and other natural relaxations preserve neither guarantee. Finding a maximum LCC is NP-hard even in the plane, and with unbounded dimension, deciding whether an LCC exists is NP-complete for every fixed k>=2. LatSweep fixes the answer's smallest tolerance and turns the coupled bound into a best-first sweep over candidate thresholds, yielding an exact branch-and-bound algorithm, a (1,2)-bicriteria approximation and two feasible heuristics. Across eight graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, six with synthetic positions and tolerances, the exact algorithm proves optimality on all but 9 of 3,700 efficiency queries; in a shared implementation on two large graphs, its branch-and-bound solver proves more queries than a reimplemented maximum-(k,r)-core algorithm, a mixed-integer program and CP-SAT. In simulations of closed groups, LCC groups keep every accepted interaction under uneven influence, whereas 3-40% of pairwise-compatible groups lose some. On three location-based networks, tolerance-agnostic groups often place another member's home beyond a member's estimated travel radius. Enforcing every member's tolerance causes no measurable loss of co-visits relative to spatial communities of the same size. Relative to the larger pairwise-compatible groups, it can cause a size-adjusted loss.

papers.title: HistogramTools for Efficient Data Analysis and Distribution Representation in Large Data Sets
papers.abstract: Histograms provide a powerful means of summarizing large data sets by representing their distribution in a compact, binned form. The HistogramTools R package enhances R built-in histogram functionality, offering advanced methods for manipulating and analyzing histograms, especially in large-scale data environments. Key features include the ability to serialize histograms using Protocol Buffers for distributed computing tasks, tools for merging and modifying histograms, and techniques for measuring and visualizing information loss in histogram representations. The package is particularly suited for environments utilizing MapReduce, where efficient storage and data sharing are critical. This paper presents various methods of histogram bin manipulation, distance measures, quantile approximation, and error estimation in cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) derived from histograms. Visualization techniques and efficient storage representations are also discussed alongside applications for large data processing and distributed computing tasks.

papers.title: Hippasus: Accurate and Cost-Efficient Feature Augmentation over Relational Tables
papers.abstract: ML models critically depend on feature quality, yet in real-world settings, useful features are often distributed across multiple relational tables rather than a single dataset. Feature augmentation addresses this problem by automatically discovering and joining additional tables to enrich a base table with predictive features. However, scaling feature augmentation to complex schemas with many tables and multi-hop relationships is challenging. It requires exploring a large space of join paths, executing costly joins, and selecting useful features from noisy results. Existing approaches suffer from either limited effectiveness or efficiency. Restricting exploration to simple joins limits predictive performance, while more expressive methods rely on expensive training data, lack scalability, or fail to fully exploit schema-level semantics. We present Hippasus, a cost-aware, LLM-guided feature augmentation framework over relational schemas, that addresses these challenges. Hippasus ranks candidate join paths before executing any join, by combining lightweight statistical signals with adaptive semantic analysis, invoking an LLM only when necessary. It further introduces efficient multi-way join execution with cross-path feature consolidation, and a hybrid feature selection strategy that integrates statistical relevance with semantic refinement. Experiments on 13 real-world datasets show that Hippasus improves predictive performance by up to 15.7% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while running on par with the fastest of them and keeping its LLM token cost low.

papers.title: StraTyper: Automated Semantic Type Discovery and Multi-Type Annotation for Dataset Collections
papers.abstract: Understanding dataset semantics is crucial for effective search, discovery, and integration pipelines. To this end, column-type annotation (CTA) methods associate columns in tabular datasets with semantic types that accurately describe their contents, using pretrained deep learning models or Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing approaches have important limitations. First, they require users to specify a closed set of semantic types either during training or inference, which hinders their application to domain-specific datasets where predefined type vocabularies often lack adequate coverage and specificity. They also assume that each column is associated with a single semantic type, an assumption that does not hold for many real-world datasets. Lastly, while proprietary LLMs have shown effectiveness for CTA, they incur high monetary costs and produce inconsistent outputs across similar columns, leading to type redundancy that degrades downstream applications. To address these challenges, we introduce StraTyper, a cost-effective method for column type discovery (CTD) and multi-type annotation (CMTA) in dataset collections. StraTyper eliminates the need for predefined semantic labels by employing LLMs to discover types tailored to the target dataset collection. Through strategic column clustering, controlled type generation, and iterative cascading discovery, StraTyper balances type precision with annotation coverage while minimizing LLM costs. Our experimental evaluation, both manual and LLM-assisted, on real-world dataset collections demonstrates that StraTyper discovers accurate types for both numeric and textual data, achieves substantial cost savings over commercial LLMs, and effectively handles multi-typed columns. We further show that StraTyper's annotations improve downstream tasks, including join discovery and schema matching, outperforming LLM-only baselines.
